title: Given an `orders(id, order_date, total_amount)` table, write a query to calculate revenue for each month (group by year and month).
shortTitle: Monthly Revenue Report — GROUP BY Year and Month
topicTitle: Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM

s1_definition.profdef: A monthly revenue report groups every order row by the calendar year and month extracted from `order_date`, then sums `total_amount` within each group. You extract the year/month with functions like `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)` and `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` (or `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`), put those in both the `SELECT` and the `GROUP BY`, aggregate with `SUM(total_amount)`, and order chronologically.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a shoebox full of order slips, each with a date and an amount. Rajesh the accountant wants to know how much money came in each month. He sorts the slips into monthly piles — all of January 2026 together, all of February 2026 together — and adds up the amounts in each pile. That sorting into month piles is `GROUP BY year, month`, and adding each pile is `SUM(total_amount)`.
s1_definition.oneliner: Extract year and month from the date, `GROUP BY` both, `SUM` the amount, and `ORDER BY` year, month for a chronological revenue report.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A monthly revenue report groups every order row by the calendar year and month extracted from `order_date`, then sums `total_amount` within each group. You extract the year/month with functions like `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)` and `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` (or `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`), put those in both the `SELECT` and the `GROUP BY`, aggregate with `SUM(total_amount)`, and order chronologically.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a shoebox full of order slips, each with a date and an amount. Rajesh the accountant wants to know how much money came in each month. He sorts the slips into monthly piles — all of January 2026 together, all of February 2026 together — and adds up the amounts in each pile. That sorting into month piles is `GROUP BY year, month`, and adding each pile is `SUM(total_amount)`.

**One line to remember:** Extract year and month from the date, `GROUP BY` both, `SUM` the amount, and `ORDER BY` year, month for a chronological revenue report.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that `GROUP BY` collapses many rows that share the same key into one output row, and an aggregate function like `SUM` computes a single value per group. For a monthly report the grouping key is the pair (year, month), so two orders placed on different days of the same month land in the same group.

There are two common ways to express the key. The portable, standard way uses `EXTRACT`: `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)` returns the year as a number and `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` returns 1 through 12. You select both, group by both, and sum the amount. For example in PostgreSQL:

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)  AS yr,
       EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS mon,
       SUM(total_amount)              AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
ORDER BY yr, mon;
```

The second way uses `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`, which rounds every timestamp down to the first day of its month, so `2026-03-15` and `2026-03-28` both become `2026-03-01`. Grouping by that single truncated value is clean and keeps results sorted naturally as a date:

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month_start,
       SUM(total_amount)               AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
ORDER BY month_start;
```

A critical rule that trips juniors up: every non-aggregated column in the `SELECT` must appear in the `GROUP BY`. You cannot select `order_date` raw alongside `SUM` unless it is in the group key, because the engine would not know which of the many dates in the group to show. Grouping by year and month separately (rather than just month) matters because otherwise January 2025 and January 2026 would be merged into one "January" bucket, which is wrong for a multi-year report.

A senior nuance is performance and correctness. If `order_date` is a timestamp with time zone, truncation and extraction happen in the session time zone unless you convert explicitly, so a report "for IST" should convert with `order_date AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` first. For large tables, an index on `order_date` helps range-limited reports (for example a single year), and in reporting warehouses you often pre-compute these monthly sums into a materialized view so the dashboard does not re-scan millions of rows every time. Also be aware `SUM` ignores `NULL` amounts, so if `total_amount` can be null you may want `SUM(COALESCE(total_amount, 0))` to treat missing as zero.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India runs a small merchant-orders platform where Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) place purchase orders funded from their accounts. The finance team needs a month-by-month revenue report to see seasonal trends and to reconcile against the general ledger. Right now someone exports a spreadsheet and manually sorts by month, which is slow and error-prone when orders span multiple years.

This is exactly what `GROUP BY year, month` with `SUM` solves — the database does the bucketing and totalling in one pass. Our mini-project builds a tiny in-memory version of the same SQL logic so you can see the grouping clearly: an `Order` record with a date and a `BigDecimal` amount, a repository holding the orders, and a `RevenueReportService` that groups orders by (year, month) and sums the amounts, mirroring the SQL exactly. The demo prints the monthly revenue for Rajesh's and Priya's orders across two years.

The code will contain: an `Order` class, an `OrderRepository` that returns all orders, a `MonthlyRevenue` result class holding year, month and total, a `RevenueReportService.monthlyRevenue()` method that performs the grouping and summing, and a `Demo` main method that loads sample orders and prints the report sorted by year then month.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five orders — two in January 2025 (12000 + 8000), one in February 2025 (15000), and two in January 2026 (20000 + 5000).

Step 1: The service calls `repo.findAll()`, which returns all five `Order` objects. In the real system this is the `orders` table being scanned or range-read by the `GROUP BY` query. The data lives as rows with a date and an amount.

Step 2: For each order, the service extracts the year and month from `orderDate` and builds a key like `"2025-01"`. This is the SQL `EXTRACT(YEAR ...)`/`EXTRACT(MONTH ...)` step — each row is tagged with which monthly bucket it belongs to. The amount stays unchanged; only the grouping tag is derived.

Step 3: The service merges each amount into a `TreeMap` keyed by that month string using `BigDecimal::add`. This is the `SUM(total_amount)` aggregation — the January 2025 bucket accumulates 12000 then 8000 to become 20000, while the February 2025 bucket holds 15000 and the January 2026 bucket accumulates 20000 then 5000 to become 25000.

Step 4: Because a `TreeMap` keeps keys in sorted order, iterating it yields `2025-01`, `2025-02`, `2026-01` in chronological order — the SQL `ORDER BY yr, mon`. Each entry is converted to a `MonthlyRevenue` object with year, month, and total.

Step 5: The application prints the three rows. The individual order amounts no longer appear; only the three monthly totals remain, which is the whole point of aggregation.

```
Oct 25, 2026 16:52:10 INFO: Built monthly revenue report with 3 months
YEAR  MONTH  REVENUE
2025   01     Rs.20000.00
2025   02     Rs.15000.00
2026   01     Rs.25000.00
```

Reports hit a read replica (never the write primary) so heavy aggregation does not slow down live order writes. A nightly-refreshed materialized view pre-computes the monthly sums for historical months that never change, and Redis caches the still-changing current month briefly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To compute revenue per month I group the orders by the year and month taken from the order date and sum the total amount within each group. In standard SQL I write `SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS yr, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS mon, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) ORDER BY yr, mon`. On PostgreSQL I often prefer `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` as a single clean grouping key that also sorts naturally. The key rule is that every non-aggregated column I select must be in the GROUP BY, and I group by year and month together so that January of different years do not collapse into one bucket.

In our National Bank of India merchant platform the finance team needed a month-by-month revenue report across multiple years to spot seasonal trends and reconcile against the ledger. I replaced a manual spreadsheet sort with this grouped query, which the database does in a single pass. The senior points I always add are that revenue reports should run against a read replica rather than the write primary, that for historical months whose totals never change I pre-compute the sums into a materialized view refreshed nightly, and that I cache the still-changing current month briefly in Redis so the dashboard is fast. I also make sure that when the date is a timestamp with time zone I convert it to the bank's reporting zone like Asia/Kolkata before truncating, and that money is always summed as a decimal type so there is no floating-point rounding error. The line I remember is: extract year and month, group by both, sum the amount, and order chronologically.

---

keyPoints: GROUP BY: group rows by column values
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
HAVING: filter groups (vs WHERE which filters rows)
GROUP BY + HAVING vs WHERE: WHERE runs first, HAVING runs after grouping
